mcqs.question: When you write <View> in a React Native component, what does that ultimately become on iOS at runtime?
options: A simulated DOM element rendered by a JavaScript-based layout engine
An actual native UIView instance, since React Native's hybrid-native model drives real platform views
An HTML div rendered inside an embedded web view
A Skia-drawn canvas element, the same approach Flutter uses
mcqs.explanation: React Native's hybrid-native strategy means React components map to real native views under the hood — <View> becomes an actual UIView on iOS — not a simulated DOM, an embedded web view, or a self-drawn canvas element like Flutter's approach.

mcqs.question: A useEffect hook reads a state variable inside its callback but that variable is missing from the dependency array. What's the risk?
options: The effect will run on every single render regardless of the dependency array's contents
The app will fail to compile, since React enforces exhaustive dependency arrays at build time
The effect can use a stale value of that variable from a previous render, since the callback isn't rerun for changes to a dependency it doesn't declare
The effect will simply never run at all
mcqs.explanation: The dependency array controls when the effect re-runs; omitting a value the callback actually reads means the effect can execute again without seeing that value's latest change, producing a stale-closure bug. It's a lint warning in most setups, not a compile error, and it doesn't mean the effect runs every render or never runs.

mcqs.question: A team needs to call a brand-new platform biometric API that React Native's built-in components don't expose. What's the standard approach?
options: Wait for a future React Native release to add built-in support
Reimplement the biometric logic entirely in JavaScript
This is not possible without ejecting to a fully native app
Write a native module in Swift/Kotlin exposing the API, called from JavaScript via the bridge or JSI
mcqs.explanation: Native modules are the standard escape hatch for reaching platform capability the framework doesn't already expose — native code implements the feature and exposes a defined interface JavaScript calls, without needing a framework release or a full native rewrite. Biometric logic specifically can't be reimplemented in pure JavaScript since it needs platform-level secure hardware access.

mcqs.question: Why does Hermes generally give faster cold-start times than JavaScriptCore for a React Native app?
options: Hermes precompiles JavaScript to bytecode ahead of time, so launch loads and runs bytecode directly instead of parsing and compiling raw JS on-device
Hermes runs on a separate CPU core dedicated entirely to JavaScript execution
JavaScriptCore requires a network connection to compile JavaScript remotely
Hermes skips executing any JavaScript during the first three seconds after launch
mcqs.explanation: Ahead-of-time bytecode compilation is the actual mechanism behind Hermes's startup advantage — the device does less work at launch since parsing and compiling already happened at build time. JavaScriptCore requires no network compilation, and neither engine uses a dedicated core or delays execution artificially.

mcqs.question: A heavy synchronous JSON-parsing loop runs directly inside a button's onPress handler, and the whole app's gestures and animations freeze for a moment when tapped. What's happening?
options: The parsing loop blocks the single JS thread, and everything depending on it — including gesture handling not otherwise offloaded to native — stalls until it finishes
This is expected behavior and cannot be avoided in React Native
The native thread itself is blocked, unrelated to the JS thread
The bridge has a hard-coded rate limit causing the freeze
mcqs.explanation: The JS thread is single-threaded and handles event handlers and component logic; a heavy synchronous computation there blocks everything else queued on that same thread, including gesture responses not specifically offloaded to native via something like reanimated worklets. This is avoidable by moving heavy work off the JS thread, and it's specifically the JS thread being blocked, not the native thread or a bridge rate limit.

mcqs.question: A component wrapped in React.memo still re-renders every time its parent renders, even though its visible props haven't logically changed. The parent passes an inline arrow function and an inline style object as props. What's the likely cause?
options: React.memo does not work with functional components, only class components
The memoized component has too many props for React.memo to handle correctly
A new function and object are created by reference on every parent render, so React's shallow prop comparison sees them as different props even though they're logically equivalent
Inline styles are not supported inside memoized components
mcqs.explanation: React.memo's shallow comparison checks reference equality, and inline function/object literals get a new reference on every render regardless of logical content, defeating the memoization silently. React.memo works fine with functional components, has no meaningful prop-count limit, and inline styles are fully supported — the reference instability is the actual cause.
